title: Water play with measuring cups
description: Pouring and comparing volumes using different-sized cups and containers. Ask: which holds more? How many small cups fill the big one?
notes: Works great with a water table or bin on the patio

title: Nature scavenger hunt
description: Give each child a list of things to find (something round, something rough, something alive). Compare finds at the end.
notes: Can be done in backyard or on a walk; adapt the list to age

title: Color mixing with paint
description: Start with primary colors only. Ask kids to predict what will happen before mixing. Document results on paper.
notes: Tempera paint is easiest to clean up

title: Story-retelling with toys
description: Read a short book, then have the child re-enact the story using toys or stuffed animals. Ask: what happened first? Then what?
notes: Works with any familiar book; encourage them to add their own ending

title: Shape sorting and building
description: Use blocks, cardboard cutouts, or household objects to sort by shape, then build something. Name the shapes as you go.

title: Lemonade stand math
description: Set prices, count money, make change. Keep it simple (everything costs 25 cents or 50 cents to start).
notes: Works best with a small neighborhood audience so transactions feel real

title: Summer journal
description: Write or draw one thing per week: something that happened, something you noticed, a question you have. No wrong answers.
notes: Drawings count fully; the habit matters more than the content

title: Draw a map of the block
description: Walk the block together first, then draw it from memory. What's on each corner? Where are your friends' houses?
notes: Compare maps with neighborhood kids — differences are the interesting part

title: Grow something and track it
description: Plant a seed (bean or sunflower works fast). Measure height weekly, note changes, predict what comes next.
notes: Takes the whole summer — start in early June. Works in a pot if no garden.

title: Card and strategy games
description: Go Fish, War, Uno, Sleeping Queens, or similar. Focus on turn-taking, counting, reading other players.
notes: Uno and Sleeping Queens work well across the 5-8 age range together

title: Backyard Olympics
description: Design 4-6 simple events (long jump, bean bag toss, balance beam, sprint). Older kids plan and run events; younger kids compete.
notes: Assign the 6-year-olds as event directors; give everyone a ribbon or sticker medal

title: Play market
description: Set up a store with priced items (toys, fruit, stickers). Older kids run the shop; younger kids shop with play money.
notes: Use index cards as price tags; keep prices to whole numbers

title: Photo walk
description: Each child gets a theme (round things, red things, things that make you happy). Walk the neighborhood and photograph finds.
notes: Parents hold phones; review and name the photos together at the end

title: Build challenge
description: Same materials, open goal: tallest tower, widest bridge, a house for a specific toy. Brief debrief: what worked, what would you change?
column13: and dry pasta are great materials. Popsicle sticks too.

title: Sensory bin exploration
description: Fill a bin with rice, sand, or dried beans. Hide small objects inside. Add cups, spoons, funnels.
notes: Best outside; rice and beans are easier to sweep than sand

title: Pattern making with objects
description: Create AB, AAB, ABC patterns using rocks, leaves, blocks, or stickers. Ask: what comes next?

title: Simple cooking or baking
description: Follow a 3-step recipe (no-bake energy balls, fruit skewers, simple salad). Focus on measuring and sequencing.
notes: No-bake recipes are easiest; focus on the measuring and sequencing not the result

title: Bug or bird journaling
description: Spend 15 minutes in the yard or park observing one type of animal. Draw it, note what it was doing, look it up together.
notes: A cheap magnifying glass makes this much more engaging

title: Sidewalk chalk math
description: Write numbers, shapes, or equations on the driveway. Hop on answers, trace shapes, play number hopscotch.

title: Neighborhood interview project
description: Each child picks one neighbor or family member to interview (3 questions they write themselves). Report back to the group.
notes: Takes two weekends: one to write questions and interview
